docs.title: Soft Skill Playbook
docs.text:
Written for software developers: the fresher on day one, and the engineer with 15 years who still dreads the CEO review.

How to talk to your manager, your juniors and your CEO. How to explain an issue and get through the day-to-day. What to say at the airport, on the train, and in the other places where you have to speak up.

Start with the Master Prompt Build Confidence

docs.title: The one-line philosophy
docs.text:
Soft skills are hard skills you practise out loud.

Nobody is born good at this. Confident communicators have prepared phrases, have practised them, and reflect on how each conversation went. This playbook gives you all three.

docs.title: Master Prompt: Your AI Communication Coach
docs.text: Use this first. Paste it into any AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, etc.) to get a coach that plays your manager, your CEO, an airport officer or anyone else you need to practise with, then gives you honest feedback.

docs.title: The master prompt
docs.text:
Copy the whole block, fill in the [brackets], and send it.

You are my personal communication and soft-skills coach. Treat it like a sparring partner, not a lecture.

ABOUT ME
- Role: [e.g. Senior Software Developer, 15 years experience]
- Level of comfort speaking: [beginner / intermediate / confident but want polish]
- First language: [e.g. Hindi]; I communicate at work in: [English]
- What I find hard: [e.g. speaking up in meetings, talking to senior leadership, saying no, small talk]
- Goal for this session: [e.g. prepare for a 1:1 where I ask for a promotion]

HOW TO RUN THE SESSION
1. Ask me up to 3 short questions to understand the situation. Don't ask more than that.
2. Then ROLE-PLAY. You play [the other person: my manager / CEO / junior / airport check-in staff /
   train TTE / interviewer]. Stay in character. Be realistic, slightly challenging but fair.
   Speak one turn at a time and wait for my reply.
3. When I type "PAUSE", step out of character and coach me on my last reply.
4. When I type "DEBRIEF", end the role-play and give feedback in this exact format:
   - What worked (2-3 points, specific quotes from me)
   - What to improve (top 3 only, most important first)
   - Rewrite: my weakest reply rewritten in 3 versions: simple, professional, confident
   - Phrases to memorise (5 max)
   - Confidence score 1-10 with one reason
   - One drill I can do tomorrow in under 10 minutes

FEEDBACK RULES
- Be direct and kind. No generic praise.
- Check clarity (was my point clear in the first sentence?), structure (context → issue → impact → ask),
  tone (polite, not submissive; firm, not rude), brevity (cut filler: "basically", "actually", "like"),
  and confidence (no over-apologising, no "I think maybe...").
- If my English grammar is wrong, correct it quietly in the rewrite. Don't make a big deal of it.
- Adapt to the listener: CEO = bottom line first; manager = status + risk + ask;
  junior = encouraging + clear next step; stranger/service staff = polite + specific.

Start now with your 3 questions.

docs.title: Ready-made variations
docs.text:
Swap the Goal and role-play lines for any of these.

ManagerCEOJuniorAirportTrainInterviewSmall talk 
Goal: tell my manager the feature will slip by 1 week because of an unplanned API dependency,
and propose two options. You play my manager, who is under pressure from their own boss.

Goal: explain yesterday's 40-minute checkout outage to the CEO in under 2 minutes, and ask for
approval to spend 2 sprints on reliability work. You play a busy, non-technical CEO who cares
about revenue and customers.

Goal: give feedback to a junior developer whose PR has no tests and poor naming, without
demotivating them. You play the junior: a bit defensive, eager to prove themselves.

Goal: practise international airport conversations: check-in with extra baggage, a security
question, immigration questions, and a delayed connecting flight. You play each officer/staff
member in turn. Speak naturally and quickly like real staff do.

Goal: practise train-station conversations: asking about a platform change, requesting a seat
swap, talking to the ticket examiner about a waitlisted ticket. You play the station staff,
a co-passenger and the TTE.

Goal: practise a senior engineer behavioural interview. Ask me 5 questions (conflict, failure,
leadership, influence without authority, a hard technical decision). Use the STAR method to
judge my answers.

Goal: practise 5 minutes of small talk at a tech conference with a stranger who turns out to be
a VP of Engineering. Help me start, keep it going, and exit politely with a LinkedIn connection.

docs.title: Mini prompts for daily use
docs.text:
When Prompt Before sending an important message Rewrite this to be clear, polite and confident. Keep it under 80 words. Put the main point first: [paste] Before a meeting I have a meeting with [person] about [topic]. Give me a 3-point structure, 2 likely objections and how to answer each. After a bad conversation Here's what happened: [story]. What could I have said instead? Give me 3 phrases for next time. Explaining tech to non-tech Explain [technical issue] to a [CEO / customer / sales team] in 3 sentences using one everyday analogy. Building vocabulary Give me 10 professional alternatives to [phrase I overuse], with an example sentence each. Confidence check Read my message. Highlight every word that sounds unsure or over-apologetic and suggest a stronger version.

Make it a habit

Do one 10-minute role-play a day for 30 days. Save the "Phrases to memorise" in a notes file. That file becomes your own phrase bank. Start from this playbook's Phrase Bank.

Privacy

Don't paste confidential code, customer data, or names of real colleagues into public AI tools. Anonymise first ("Person A", "Service X").

docs.title: Appraisal Discussion
docs.text:
The appraisal is where your rating turns into money: the hike, the bonus, sometimes a new title. Find out how the numbers were decided, respond with data rather than emotion, and leave with either an improvement or a written plan.

Appraisal vs performance review

The Performance Review is about feedback and rating. The appraisal discussion is about the outcome: hike %, bonus, promotion, and what happens if you disagree. In many companies they happen in the same meeting; prepare for both.

docs.title: Before the discussion
docs.text: 1. Know the system — rating scale, hike bands, bonus formula, promotion cycle 2. Know your market — what your role pays outside (see Salary Negotiation) 3. Know your case — top 3–5 wins with numbers (your wins file) 4. Know your ask — the specific hike/title you think is fair 5. Know your floor — what you'll do if the outcome is below it

docs.title: Questions to research (or ask HR) beforehand
docs.text:
• How are hike percentages linked to ratings? Is there a range per rating?
  • Is there a separate market correction budget for people paid below band?
  • How is the variable bonus calculated (company %, individual %)?
  • When is the promotion cycle, and is promotion a separate hike?
  • Can a rating or hike be reviewed or appealed? Who decides?

docs.title: Understanding your hike letter
docs.text:
Item Ask yourself Fixed pay increase % Is it above or below inflation (~5–6%) and the company average? New CTC breakdown Did fixed go up, or only variable/benefits? Variable / bonus Target vs actual payout %? When is it paid? ESOPs / RSUs New grant? Vesting schedule? Effective date Is it backdated (arrears)? Title / level Did your level change, or just the title?

Watch the CTC trick

A "15% CTC hike" can mean only 8% more fixed pay if the rest is variable, insurance or gratuity. Always compare monthly in-hand and fixed pay year on year.

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
Good outcomeHike below expectationManager says \"It's out of my hands\"Promised promotion didn't happenRating and hike don't matchAsking for non-cash alternatives

"Thank you, I really appreciate this and the recognition. I'd like to keep this momentum. What should I focus on so I'm considered for promotion in the next cycle?"

"Thank you for walking me through this. I'll be honest: the hike is lower than I expected given my rating and impact. This year I led the checkout migration and cut cloud costs by ₹35 lakh. Could you help me understand how the number was decided?"

Then:

"Based on market data for my role, I'm currently about 15% below the range. Is there a possibility of a market correction, either now or at the mid-year review?"

"I understand budgets are set centrally. Could you take my case to HR / your manager for a correction? I'm happy to put the details in writing so it's easy to share. And if nothing can change now, could we agree in writing on a review in 6 months with clear criteria?"

"Last cycle we agreed that leading the platform migration would make the case for promotion. I delivered it in September. What changed? I'd like to understand the gap, and get a specific timeline and criteria in writing this time."

"My rating is 'Exceeds Expectations', but the hike is close to the company average. Is the hike band for my rating different from what I understood? I want to make sure there's no error before we close this."

Mistakes do happen in the system. Asking politely is fine.

"If the fixed hike can't change, could we look at a one-time bonus, an extra ESOP grant, a certification budget, or a title change? Any of these would show recognition of this year's work."

docs.title: Escalating properly (if the outcome is clearly unfair)
docs.text:
1. Sleep on it. Don't react in the meeting or on Slack.
  2. Ask your manager for the reasoning in writing.
  3. Write a calm, factual email with your achievements and data.
  4. Use the official review / appeal process (HR, skip-level).
  5. Decide on your floor. If it isn't met, start planning quietly and professionally.
Subject: Request to review my appraisal outcome

Hi Priya,

Thank you for our discussion today. As mentioned, I'd like to request a review of my
appraisal outcome. Summary:

• Rating: Exceeds Expectations
• Key outcomes: checkout migration (−60% failed orders), ₹35L/yr cloud savings,
  mentored 4 engineers (2 promoted)
• Market data: current fixed pay is ~15% below the range for Senior Engineer in Bangalore

I'd appreciate it if this could be considered for a correction, or a defined review at
mid-year. Happy to discuss further.

Best regards,
Ashish

docs.title: Phrases that help and phrases that hurt
docs.text: ❌ Avoid ✅ Use instead "This is unfair, everyone else got more." "Can you help me understand how this was decided?" "I'll leave if this doesn't change." "I want to build my career here. What would it take?" "My friend at X got 40%." "Market data for my role shows a range of…" Silent acceptance, then complaining later "Can I take a day to think about this and come back to you?" Discussing your hike with teammates Keep your numbers private; it's usually company policy too.

docs.title: For team leads delivering appraisals
docs.text:
• Know the numbers before the meeting: the band, the reasoning, what's flexible and what isn't.
  • Lead with the outcome, then the reasoning. Don't make people wait 20 minutes for the number.
  • Don't blame "management" for numbers you supported. If you fought for more, you can say so.
  • Allow emotion: "I understand this is disappointing. Take your time."
  • Never promise what you can't guarantee ("Next year for sure").
  • End with a clear growth plan and a check-in date.

docs.title: First 90 Days at a New Job
docs.text: First impressions are formed in weeks and last for years. Spend the first 90 days listening, building relationships, and delivering one visible early win.

docs.title: The 30-60-90 plan
docs.text: Days 1–30: Learn — people, product, codebase, how decisions get made Days 31–60: Contribute — ship real work, join discussions, own something small Days 61–90: Lead — propose improvements, own a feature, mentor where you can

docs.title: Introducing yourself
docs.text:
To the team (stand-up / first meeting)Slack / Teams introTo your new manager (first 1:1)

"Hi everyone, I'm Ashish. I've joined as a senior backend engineer. Before this, I spent 6 years building payment systems at XYZ. Outside work, I love cricket and cooking. I'm looking forward to learning how things work here, so please bear with my questions!" 

👋 Hi all! I'm Ashish, joining the Checkout team as a Senior Backend Engineer.
Previously: 6 yrs on payments at XYZ (Java, Kafka, Postgres).
Fun fact: I've visited 14 states on train journeys 🚆
Would love a 15-min coffee chat with anyone. Happy to learn how your team works!
  • "What does success look like for me at 30, 60 and 90 days?"
  • "How do you prefer to communicate: Slack, email, 1:1s? How often do you want updates?"
  • "Who are the key people I should meet in my first month?"
  • "What's the biggest challenge the team faces right now?"
  • "Is there a small, valuable task I could pick up as a first win?"

docs.title: Questions to ask in your first month
docs.text: Area Questions Product "Who are our users? What do they complain about most?" Codebase "Which parts are fragile? Where is the documentation?" Process "How does code go from PR to production? What's the on-call setup?" People "Who's the go-to person for payments / infra / data?" Culture "How are decisions made? How do people disagree here?" History "Why was it built this way?" (ask out of curiosity, not to judge)

docs.title: Senior hires: avoid the classic trap
docs.text:
Don't start with \"At my last company we did it better…\"

Even when you're right, it sounds like criticism. Try:

  • "Help me understand why we chose this approach."
  • "I've seen a pattern that worked well for this problem. Would it be useful if I wrote it up?"
  • Earn trust with small wins first; propose big changes after 60 days.

docs.title: Habits for the first 90 days
docs.text:
• Take notes in every meeting; start a personal "how things work here" doc
  • Coffee chats: 2 per week with people across teams
  • Fix the onboarding docs wherever you hit a gap (an easy first PR)
  • Ship your first PR in week 1, even if it's tiny
  • Send a weekly update to your manager for the first 2 months
  • Ask for feedback at day 30: "How am I doing? Anything I should adjust?"
  • Remember names: say them back when introduced, and write them down after

docs.title: Day-90 conversation with your manager
docs.text: "It's been 90 days, and I'd like to reflect together. Here's what I've delivered: the coupon validator and the on-call runbook. Here's what I've learned about the team. What's your feedback, and what should my priorities be for the next 6 months?"

docs.title: Handling Layoffs
docs.text:
A layoff is a business decision. It is not a judgement of your worth. Many good engineers, at every level, have been laid off. This page covers what to say and ask on the day, how to talk about it with family and future employers, how to support colleagues, and how leads can deliver the news humanely.

Your rights vary

Severance, notice and benefits depend on your country, state, contract and company policy. Use this page as a communication guide, and get advice from HR or an employment lawyer about your specific situation before you sign anything.

docs.title: On the day: the meeting
docs.text:
Layoff meetings are often short (10–15 minutes), with your manager and/or HR. You don't need to argue or decide anything in the room.

1. Breathe — it's okay to be shocked; you can take a moment 2. Listen — take notes, or ask for everything in writing 3. Ask key questions — see the list below 4. Don't sign immediately — ask how long you have to review 5. Leave with dignity — people remember this moment

"I understand. This is a lot to take in. Could you send me all the details in writing? I'd like to review the agreement properly before signing. How many days do I have?"

docs.title: Questions to ask HR
docs.text:
Area Questions Last day & pay What's my last working day? Will I get notice pay, or garden leave? When is the final settlement paid? Severance How is the severance calculated? Is it negotiable? Is it tied to signing a release? Leave & bonus Will unused leave be paid out? Any pro-rated bonus? Equity What happens to unvested ESOPs/RSUs? How long do I have to exercise vested options? Insurance How long does health insurance continue? Can I convert it to a personal policy? Documents When will I get the relieving letter, experience letter and payslips? Reason How will this be described to future employers (layoff / role eliminated)? Will you provide a reference? Visa (if applicable) How does this affect my work visa? What is the grace period? Support Is there outplacement support, career coaching, or counselling? Equipment How and when do I return the laptop? Can I save personal files?

Things to save (personal items only)

Your payslips, offer letter, appraisal letters, and personal contacts. Write down your achievements while you still remember them. Never take company code, documents or customer data.

docs.title: Negotiating the package (politely)
docs.text:
"Thank you for the offer. Given my 6 years here and the time it may take to find a similar role, would it be possible to extend the severance by one month, or extend health insurance until March? I'd appreciate it if you could check."

It doesn't always work, but asking politely, once, is reasonable.

docs.title: Telling people
docs.text:
Your familyYour colleagues (farewell message)LinkedIn post

"I have some difficult news: my company did layoffs today, and my role was affected. It's not about my performance. Around 200 people were let go. We have [X months] of savings and a severance package, and I'm going to start looking right away. I'll need your support."

Be honest, share the plan, and let them help.

Hi everyone,
As some of you know, my role was affected by today's layoffs. I'm grateful for the 6 years
here and especially for this team: the sale-day war rooms, the code reviews, the chai.
I'm now open to Senior Backend / Tech Lead roles. Referrals or intros would mean a lot.
Stay in touch: linkedin.com/in/ashish-example · ashish.personal@example.com

After 6 great years at XYZ, my role was impacted by this week's layoffs.

I'm proud of what we built: the checkout platform that handled 10x sale-day traffic, and
a team culture I'll miss.

I'm now looking for Senior Backend Engineer / Tech Lead roles (Java, Kafka, distributed
systems) in Bangalore or remote. If you know of an opportunity, I'd be grateful for a
referral or introduction.

#OpenToWork

Keep it positive, specific and forward-looking. Never criticise the company.

docs.title: Talking about it in interviews
docs.text:
"My role was part of a company-wide layoff that affected about 15% of engineering, after the company changed strategy. I'm proud of my time there: I led the checkout re-architecture. I'm now looking for a team where I can [your goal], which is why this role interests me."

  • Say it once, briefly and calmly. There's nothing to be ashamed of, and interviewers know layoffs are common.
  • Move quickly to what you achieved and what you're looking for.
  • If asked about a gap: "I took a few weeks to rest and upskill on Kubernetes, then started interviewing."

docs.title: Looking after yourself
docs.text:
• Take a few days to process before job-hunting hard.
  • Keep a routine: fixed hours for applications, learning, exercise, and rest.
  • Reach out: former managers and colleagues are your strongest source of referrals.
  • Set small daily goals: 3 applications, 1 networking message, 1 hour of practice.
  • Talk to someone (friends, family, a counsellor) if it's affecting your sleep or mood.
  • Remember: this is a chapter, not your whole story.

docs.title: If you survive a layoff
docs.text:
Staying can be hard too: guilt, fear, more work.

  • Reach out to colleagues who left: offer references, introductions, and a message of support.
  • Ask your manager directly:

"This has been a hard week for everyone. Can you share what this means for our team's priorities, and for the work that's been left behind? I want to focus on the right things."

  • Be honest about workload: "With 2 fewer people, we can't deliver all of this. What should we drop?"
  • Look after your own career: update your CV and wins file, without panic.

docs.title: For managers delivering layoff news
docs.text:
This is one of the hardest conversations in management. Do it with humanity.

Before:

  • Know all the facts: package, dates, benefits, the HR contact
  • Do it in person or on video, privately, never by email or in a group call first
  • Do it early in the week and day, not on a Friday evening
  • Have HR present, or immediately available
  • Plan who tells the remaining team and when

The conversation:

"Arun, thanks for joining. I have difficult news, and I want to be direct with you. Your role is being eliminated as part of the company-wide layoffs. Your last working day is the 30th. This decision was about budgets and strategy. It is not about your performance. I'm sorry. I know this is hard to hear. Sunita from HR will walk you through the package. And I will personally give you a strong reference and help with introductions."

✅ Do ❌ Don't Get to the point within the first minute Small talk before the news Say clearly that it's a business decision (if true) Say "I know how you feel" Allow silence and emotion Argue, defend, or debate the decision Offer concrete help (references, intros) Make promises you can't keep Follow up a day or two later Disappear after the meeting

Telling the remaining team:

"As you've heard, Arun and Priya were affected by today's layoffs. They were valued members of this team, and this wasn't about their work. I know this is unsettling. Here's what I know about our team's future, and here's what I don't know yet. My door is open, and we'll re-plan our priorities together tomorrow."

docs.title: Interviews
docs.text: An interview is a structured conversation between two people deciding whether to work together. You're interviewing them too. Prepare stories, not memorised answers.

docs.title: "Tell me about yourself" (60–90 seconds)
docs.text:
Present → Past → Future

"I'm a backend engineer with 15 years of experience, currently leading a team of 6 building a grocery marketplace on Java and Kafka (present). Before that, I spent 8 years in fintech, where I scaled a payments platform to 2 million transactions a day (past). I'm looking for a role where I can shape architecture and grow engineers at a larger scale, and that's what drew me to this team (future)."

Beginner version

"I recently graduated in Computer Science, and I interned at XYZ, where I built a REST API for inventory tracking in Spring Boot. I enjoy backend work and learning how systems scale, and I'm excited about this role because your team works with Kafka and microservices."

docs.title: Behavioural questions: STAR
docs.text:
Prepare 6–8 stories that you can adapt:

Theme Example question Conflict "Tell me about a disagreement with a teammate." Failure "Tell me about a time you failed." Leadership "When did you lead without authority?" Pressure "Describe a tight deadline you handled." Impact "What's the project you're proudest of?" Learning "When did you learn something quickly?" Feedback "Tell me about critical feedback you received." Decision "Describe a hard technical trade-off."

STAR answer (failure)

S: Our release went out with a data-migration bug that corrupted 2% of user addresses. T: As tech lead, I owned the fix and the follow-up. A: I rolled back within 20 minutes, wrote a repair script, personally emailed affected users, and added migration dry-runs to CI. R: All data restored in 4 hours; no repeat in 2 years. What I learned: never run migrations without a dry-run on a production snapshot.

docs.title: Questions to ask the interviewer
docs.text:
• "What does success look like in the first 90 days?"
  • "What's the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?"
  • "How are technical decisions made here?"
  • "How do engineers grow here? What did the last promotion look like?"
  • "What do you personally enjoy most about working here?"

docs.title: Handling tricky moments
docs.text: Moment Say You don't know the answer "I haven't worked with that directly. Here's how I'd approach it…" You need time to think "Let me take a moment to think about that." Salary question (early) "I'd like to learn more about the role first. What's the budgeted range?" "Why are you leaving?" Stay positive: "I'm looking for bigger scale and ownership." Never criticise your current employer. "Any weaknesses?" A real one + what you're doing about it: "I used to over-explain to executives. I now practise one-sentence summaries."

docs.title: Performance Review
docs.text: Your rating is mostly decided before the meeting. It depends on what you did all year and how well your manager knows about it. Track your wins, write a strong self-review, and treat the conversation as planning for next year, not a verdict.

docs.title: The review cycle
docs.text: 1. All year — keep a wins file; align on goals; ask for feedback every quarter 2. Self-assessment — write it with impact and numbers 3. Peer feedback — choose reviewers wisely; write good reviews for others 4. Review meeting — listen, clarify, discuss, agree on goals 5. After — follow-up in writing; act on feedback; check in at 3 months

docs.title: All year: the wins file
docs.text:
A simple note you update every Friday (5 minutes):

## Nov 2026
- Shipped coupon validation → stopped ~₹40k/week leakage (PR #212)
- Led incident response for checkout outage; wrote post-mortem; 2 fixes shipped
- Mentored Kavya on Kafka; she now owns the consumer service
- Praise: "Clearest incident updates I've seen" — VP Eng, Slack, 12 Nov

No surprises, in either direction

Ask your manager every quarter: "If reviews were today, where would I land, and what would move me up?" That way, the review meeting doesn't surprise you.

docs.title: Writing your self-assessment
docs.text:
Use Action → Impact → Evidence for every point:

❌ Weak ✅ Strong "Worked on the checkout service." "Re-architected checkout to use the outbox pattern, cutting failed orders by 60% (dashboard link)." "Helped juniors." "Mentored 3 engineers with weekly sessions; 2 now independently own services." "Fixed many bugs." "Closed 48 bugs, including 5 P1s; reduced support tickets by 30%." "Good team player." "Unblocked the payments team twice by building a shared test harness, saving ~2 weeks."

docs.title: Self-assessment template
docs.text:
## Key achievements (3–5)
1. [Action] → [Impact with number] → [Evidence/link]

## Goals from last cycle
| Goal | Result | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Reduce p95 latency < 500 ms | 420 ms | ✅ Met |
| Lead one design review | Led 3 | ✅ Exceeded |
| Get AWS certification | Postponed (release crunch) | ⚠️ Moved to Q1 |

## Growth & learning
- What I learned, what I'd do differently

## Areas to improve
- One or two honest areas + what I'm already doing about them

## Goals for next cycle
- 2–4 specific, measurable goals, ideally tied to team goals

## Support I need
- e.g. more exposure to architecture decisions; conference budget

Common self-review mistakes

Listing tasks instead of impact · being too modest ("I just helped a bit") · being vague about misses · forgetting work from early in the year (that's what the wins file is for) · writing 10 pages. Keep it to 1–2.

docs.title: Peer reviews
docs.text:
Giving peer feedbackChoosing your reviewers

Be specific, balanced and useful:

Strengths: Meena's incident leadership during the October outage was outstanding.
Clear updates every 20 minutes kept leadership calm, and the post-mortem led to
real fixes.

To grow: In design reviews she sometimes moves to a solution before the
problem is fully discussed. Pausing to ask "what else could we do?" would bring
in more ideas from the team.
  • People who saw your best work closely
  • At least one person from another team (shows cross-team impact)
  • Ask them nicely, with context: "Would you be open to reviewing me? It'd help if you could mention the search migration we did together."

docs.title: Mindset
docs.text: Go in calm and curious. Your goal is to understand the feedback and agree on a plan, not to win an argument.

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
OpeningGood reviewAsking for clarityDisagreeing with the ratingUnexpected negative feedbackAsking about promotionAsking about compensation

"Thanks for taking the time. I'd like to hear your feedback first, and then I'd love to talk about goals and what the next level looks like for me."

"Thank you, that means a lot. What would it take to get to the next level over the next cycle? I'd like to make sure I'm working on the right things."

Even with a great rating, ask for one thing to improve.

"You mentioned I need to 'show more ownership.' Could you give me an example where I could have done that differently? I want to make sure I understand what it looks like."

"I appreciate the feedback. I see some of it differently, and I'd like to share why. I led the checkout migration end to end, which was one of the team's top goals, and it reduced failures by 60%. Could you help me understand how that was weighed?"

Then, if it still feels unfair:

"I'd like some time to reflect on this. Could we follow up later this week? And what's the process if I'd like the rating reconsidered?"

Don't

Raise your voice · compare yourself to named colleagues ("But Rahul got…") · threaten to quit · cry foul in team channels. Stay factual and calm, and put things in writing.

  1. Pause and breathe. You don't need to respond instantly.
  2. "Thank you for being direct. This is hard to hear, but I want to understand."
  3. "Can you share specific examples?"
  4. "What would 'good' look like in the next 3 months?"
  5. "Can we check in monthly on this?"

"I'd like to be considered for promotion to Staff Engineer. What gaps do you see between my work and that level? Could we write down 2–3 concrete goals and a timeline, and check progress quarterly?"

"How does this rating translate into my compensation? Given my impact this year and the market for my role, I'd like to discuss whether there's room for an adjustment."

See Salary Negotiation for full scripts.

docs.title: Questions to ask in every review
docs.text:
• "What's the one thing that would most increase my impact next year?"
  • "What do you see as my biggest strength, and am I using it enough?"
  • "How do others (peers, stakeholders) see my work?"
  • "What does the next level look like in practice?"
  • "How can you support me in getting there?"

docs.title: After the review
docs.text:
• Send a short summary email within 24 hours (feedback, goals, agreed support)
  • Turn feedback into 2–3 goals with measurable outcomes
  • Put a 3-month check-in in the calendar
  • Start next year's wins file today
Subject: Summary of our performance review

Hi Priya, thanks for the review today. To summarise:
• Strengths: incident leadership, mentoring
• Focus areas: earlier risk communication, more design-doc writing
• Goals: lead 2 design docs; flag schedule risks within 2 days
• Next step: check-in on 15 Feb; promotion discussion in the next cycle
Let me know if I've missed anything.

docs.title: When you're the reviewer (team leads & managers)
docs.text:
• Prepare

    Gather evidence across the whole year, not just the last month. Read their self-review first.

  • No surprises

    Nothing in the review should be news. Hard feedback belongs in regular 1:1s.

  • Specific & fair

    Use SBI (Situation-Behaviour-Impact). Judge outcomes and behaviour, not personality.

  • Forward-looking

    Spend half the time on growth and next-cycle goals.

"Your rating this cycle is Meets Expectations. Strength: your code quality and reliability work, especially the retry framework. To grow to the next level: I'd like to see you drive decisions in design reviews, not just contribute. Let's set one goal around that and check in every month. What support would help?"

docs.title: Promotion Discussion
docs.text:
Promotions are rarely given for doing your current job well. They come from showing you already work at the next level, and from making sure the people who decide can see it. Ask early, agree on criteria, gather evidence, and get your manager to argue your case for you.

How this differs from related pages

Performance Review covers your rating · Appraisal Discussion covers the hike · this page covers moving up a level: the months-long conversation that leads to it, and what to do when the answer is "not yet".

docs.title: How promotions actually work
docs.text:
1. Criteria — the company's level definitions (career ladder) 2. Evidence — sustained work at the next level, usually 6–12 months 3. Sponsor — your manager (and ideally a skip-level) who argues your case 4. Committee / calibration — managers compare cases; often you're not in the room 5. Budget & timing — cycles, headcount, open roles

The key insight: you're not in the room when the decision is made. Your job is to give your manager a case so clear they can argue it in two minutes.

docs.title: What typically changes between levels
docs.text:
From → To The shift Evidence that shows it Junior → Mid From "needs guidance" to "works independently" Delivers features end to end with little help Mid → Senior From "delivers tasks" to "owns outcomes" Owns a service/feature area; makes good design calls; mentors Senior → Staff / Lead From "owns a component" to "shapes the team or several teams" Drives cross-team technical direction; multiplies others; solves ambiguous problems Engineer → Manager From "my output" to "the team's output" Has led people informally; handles conflict; hires; gives feedback well

Get your company's ladder

Ask your manager or HR for the written level expectations. If there are none, write down together what the next level means at your company. Without written criteria, the decision becomes subjective.

docs.title: The promotion conversation, step by step
docs.text:
1. Starting the conversation (6–12 months before)2. Agreeing on criteria3. Regular check-ins4. Ask for a sponsor5. Asking directly at cycle time

"I'd like to work towards Senior Engineer. Could you help me understand what the gap is between where I am now and that level? I'd like to agree on 2–3 concrete things I can work on, and check in on them regularly."

Ask this early, not two weeks before the promotion cycle.

"So, to summarise: lead the design and delivery of the delivery-slot service, mentor at least one engineer, and lead incident response independently. If I do those well by June, would that make a strong case? Can I write this down and share it with you?"

Then send a short email so you both have a written record.

"Quick promotion check-in: I've completed the slot-service design and it's in production. Mentoring with Kavya is going well. On a scale of 1–10, how close am I to the case we discussed? What's missing?"

Do this monthly or quarterly in your 1:1.

"Would you be willing to put me forward in this cycle? I've drafted a promotion document with the evidence. Could you review it and tell me what would make it stronger?"

Also ask for visibility: "Could I present the slot-service design at the architecture review?" Committee members should know your work before your name comes up.

"The promotion cycle opens next month. I believe I'm working at the senior level, and I'd like to be considered. Here's my summary of the evidence against the criteria we agreed on. Do you agree, and are you comfortable nominating me?"

docs.title: The promotion document (brag doc)
docs.text:
Make your manager's job easy: one page, mapped to the criteria.

# Promotion case — Ashish Gupta → Senior Engineer

## Summary (3 lines)
Has operated at senior level for ~9 months: owns the delivery-slot service end to end,
leads incidents, and mentors two engineers.

## Evidence against criteria
| Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Technical ownership | Designed & shipped slot service (design doc link); 99.95% uptime since launch |
| Scope & impact | Enabled 3 new cities; reduced failed deliveries 18% |
| Influence | Led 3 design reviews; proposal adopted by payments team |
| Mentoring | Mentored Kavya & Arun; Kavya now owns consumer service |
| Operational excellence | Incident lead for 4 SEV-2s; post-mortems with 9 follow-ups shipped |

## Feedback from others
- "Ashish's design review raised the bar for the whole team." — Staff Engineer, Platform
- "Best incident communication I've seen." — VP Engineering

## Areas still growing
- Cross-org influence: starting with the 2027 architecture working group

docs.title: When the answer is "not yet"
docs.text:
Get specificsGet a commitmentRepeated \"not yet\"

"I'm disappointed, but I want to use this well. What specifically was missing in my case? Was it the evidence, the criteria, or timing and budget?"

Those are three different problems:

Reason What it means Your move Evidence gap You aren't yet doing the next-level work Agree on concrete projects that close the gap Visibility gap You did it, but the deciders didn't see it Present work, write docs, get skip-level exposure Budget / timing Case is fine, there's no slot Get the commitment in writing for the next cycle

"If I close those gaps, can we agree I'll be put forward next cycle? I'd like to write down the specific goals and review them every month together."

"This is the second cycle where the goals were met but the promotion didn't happen. I want to grow here, and I'd like to understand honestly whether a promotion is realistic in the next 6 months. If not, I'd appreciate knowing why."

Ask honestly and calmly. If the honest answer is "no", you have a decision to make: see Resignation, and leave well if that's your choice.

Don't

  • Compare yourself to named colleagues ("Rahul got promoted, why not me?")
  • Use a resignation threat as a lever, unless you're truly ready to leave
  • Go silent and resentful; ask for specifics instead
  • Expect a promotion for tenure alone ("I've been here 4 years")

docs.title: After you're promoted
docs.text:
• Thank your manager and sponsors, and the people who helped.
  • Ask: "What does great look like at this new level, in the first 6 months?"
  • Expect to feel out of your depth at first. That's normal; it's what growth feels like.
  • Help someone else get their promotion. Sponsoring others is part of being senior.

docs.title: For leads: sponsoring your people
docs.text:
• Have the career conversation with every report at least twice a year.
  • Turn the level definitions into concrete, personal goals.
  • Create opportunities: give stretch projects and visibility, and mention their names in rooms they're not in.
  • Be honest about the gap and about timing. False hope damages trust more than "not yet".
  • Write the case together, and tell them the outcome personally before any announcement.

docs.title: Resignation Conversation
docs.text: People remember how you left more than how you joined. Make the decision first, tell your manager before anyone else, be grateful and brief, hand over properly, and leave everyone glad they worked with you.

docs.title: The resignation path
docs.text: 1. Decide — offer letter signed; you're sure; you know your notice period 2. Tell your manager — in person or on video, never first by email 3. Put it in writing — short, polite resignation email 4. Handle the counter-offer — decide beforehand what you'll do 5. Serve the notice — hand over, document, stay professional 6. Exit well — exit interview, farewell, stay connected

docs.title: Before you resign: checklist
docs.text:
• Signed offer letter from the new company (not just a verbal offer)
  • Notice period and buyout rules checked in your contract
  • Unused leave, pending bonus or ESOP vesting dates checked; is it worth waiting a few weeks?
  • Personal files removed from company devices (only personal files, never company data)
  • Your reason in one positive sentence
  • Your answer to a counter-offer decided

docs.title: Telling your manager
docs.text:
Asking for the meetingThe conversation\"Why are you leaving?\"\"Where are you going?\"Manager reacts badly

"Hi Priya, do you have 15 minutes today for a private conversation? Something I'd like to discuss in person."

"Thank you for making time. I've decided to resign. I've accepted an offer from another company, and my last working day would be 3rd February, per my notice period. This wasn't an easy decision. I've learned a lot here, especially from you: the checkout migration and leading the team were big growth steps for me. I want to make the transition as smooth as possible. I'll prepare a handover plan by Friday."

Keep it short, positive and final. You're informing them, not asking permission.

"It's an opportunity to work on larger-scale systems and move into an architect role, which is the direction I want to grow in."

One positive, forward-looking reason. Don't list complaints in this meeting, even if you have them. Save constructive feedback for the exit interview, and keep it gentle.

"I'd prefer to share that closer to my last day, once everything is finalised. I hope you understand."

or simply tell them if you're comfortable. Both are fine.

"I understand this comes at a hard time, and I'm sorry about the timing. I'm committed to a proper handover and will do everything I can to reduce the impact on the team."

Stay calm. Don't argue or justify yourself at length.

docs.title: The resignation email
docs.text:
Subject: Resignation — Ashish Gupta

Dear Priya,

Please accept this email as formal notice of my resignation from my position as Senior
Software Engineer at XYZ Technologies. As per my notice period, my last working day will be
3 February 2027.

Thank you for the opportunities and support over the past four years. I'm grateful for
everything I've learned here, and I'll do my best to ensure a smooth handover.

Best regards,
Ashish Gupta

Keep it short, factual, and grateful. No reasons, no complaints. This email goes into your permanent HR record.

docs.title: Handling the counter-offer
docs.text:
Question Think about Why did I start looking? Will more money fix that (manager, growth, tech, culture)? Why is the offer coming now? Why wasn't I valued this way before I resigned? How will I be seen? Some leaders will now see you as a flight risk. What about the new company? Backing out after accepting damages your reputation there. Declining the counter-offerIf you genuinely want to consider it

"Thank you, I really appreciate the offer, and it means a lot that you want me to stay. I've thought carefully, and I've made my decision. My reasons are about the role and growth, not just compensation."

"Thank you. Can I have until tomorrow to think it over? I want to make the right decision for everyone."

Be honest with both companies and decide quickly.

docs.title: Notice period: leaving well
docs.text:
• Handover document: systems you own, credentials process, ongoing work, known issues, contacts
  • Knowledge-transfer sessions recorded for the team
  • Finish or cleanly hand over in-progress tickets; don't start big new work
  • Update runbooks / READMEs for anything only you know
  • Stay fully engaged until your last day. People notice.
  • Ask about a notice buyout or early release politely if the new company needs you sooner

"Would it be possible to be released on 20th January instead of 3rd February? I've planned the handover so it would be complete by then, and I'm happy to be available for questions afterwards."

docs.title: Exit interview
docs.text:
Be honest but constructive. Focus on systems, not people:

❌ Avoid ✅ Say instead "My manager is terrible." "More regular feedback and clearer growth paths would help people stay." "Everything here is broken." "Investing in on-call tooling would reduce burnout." "The pay is a joke." "Compensation was below market for my role, which was a factor."

docs.title: Farewell message
docs.text:
Hi everyone,

Today is my last day at XYZ. It's been an amazing four years. I've learned so much from this
team, from late-night sale days to the checkout migration we pulled off together.

Thank you for the support, the code reviews, and the chai breaks. I'll miss you all!

Let's stay in touch: linkedin.com/in/ashish-example · ashish.personal@example.com

All the best,
Ashish

docs.title: Don'ts
docs.text:
Never

  • Announce your resignation to the team before your manager knows
  • Post about it on LinkedIn before your last day (or before your manager agrees on timing)
  • Take company code, documents or customer data, even "for reference"
  • Badmouth the company or colleagues, in the office or online
  • Mentally check out during notice; it's the last thing people remember
  • Try to recruit teammates to your new company during notice

docs.title: For team leads: when someone resigns
docs.text:
• Thank them and congratulate them, even if it hurts: "I'm sad to lose you, but this is a great step."
  • Ask once if there's anything that would change their mind, then respect the answer.
  • Ask: "What could we have done better?" Listen; don't defend.
  • Plan the handover together and tell the team with them, in a positive way.
  • Celebrate their exit. Alumni can become referrals, clients, or future re-hires.

docs.title: Salary Negotiation
docs.text: Companies expect you to negotiate, and a calm, data-backed ask is professional, not rude. A few uncomfortable minutes can change your earnings for years, because every future raise builds on this number.

docs.title: The negotiation flow
docs.text: 1. Research — know your market value (range, not a single number) 2. Prepare — your wins, your target, your walk-away number 3. Delay the number — let them anchor first when possible 4. Respond — thank, show enthusiasm, then counter with data 5. Trade — negotiate the whole package, not only base pay 6. Close — confirm everything in writing

docs.title: Step 1: Know your numbers
docs.text:
Number What it means Example Market range What similar roles pay (level, city, company type) ₹45–60 LPA Target What you'll ask for: upper part of the range, backed by data ₹58 LPA Walk-away Below this, you decline. Decide before the conversation. ₹50 LPA

Sources: salary sites (Glassdoor, AmbitionBox, Levels.fyi), recruiters, trusted peers, industry reports. Compare the same level and city, and compare total compensation, not just base.

docs.title: Step 2: Build your value case
docs.text:
Write down 3–5 achievements with numbers:

  • "Led the checkout re-architecture, which cut failures 60% and protected ~₹2 Cr in sale-day revenue."
  • "Reduced cloud costs by ₹35 lakh/year."
  • "Mentored 4 engineers; 2 were promoted."
  • "Cut deploy time from 2 hours to 18 minutes."

docs.title: Scripts: new job offer
docs.text:
\"What are your salary expectations?\" (early)\"What's your current salary?\"Responding to the offerThey say \"This is our best offer\"Competing offerAccepting

"I'd like to understand the role and responsibilities better first. Could you share the budgeted range for this position?"

If they insist:

"Based on my research for senior backend roles in Bangalore with my experience, I'm looking in the range of ₹55 to 62 lakh total compensation, depending on the overall package."

Give a range whose bottom is still a number you'd be happy with.

"I'd prefer to focus on the value of this role. My expectation is based on the market and what I bring, which is around ₹58 lakh."

(In some places, employers may ask for payslips. Be honest if you share. Never inflate.)

"Thank you, I'm really excited about this role and the team. I've reviewed the offer. Given my experience leading high-scale payment systems and the market range for this level, I was expecting closer to ₹58 lakh. Is there flexibility on the base?"

Then stop talking and let them respond. The silence works in your favour.

"I understand the base may be fixed. Could we look at other parts of the package: a joining bonus, extra ESOPs, or a salary review after 6 months instead of 12?"

"I want to be transparent: I have another offer at ₹60 lakh. This role is my first choice because of the product and the team. If you can get closer to that, I'm ready to accept this week."

Only say this if it's true. Bluffing can backfire badly.

"Thank you, that works for me. I'm happy to accept. Could you send the updated offer letter with the base, joining bonus and ESOP details so I can sign it?"

docs.title: Scripts: raise at your current company
docs.text:
Asking for the meetingMaking the caseIf the answer is \"not now\"

"Could we set up 30 minutes next week to discuss my compensation and growth? I'd like to prepare properly, so I wanted to give you notice."

"Over the last year I've led the checkout migration, reduced cloud costs by ₹35 lakh, and mentored four engineers. My responsibilities have grown to include architecture for two teams. Based on that and market data for this level, I'd like to discuss an adjustment to around ₹58 lakh. What would it take to make that happen?"

"I understand the budget timing. Could we agree on specific goals and a date to revisit, say in 3 months? I'd also appreciate it in writing so we're both clear."

docs.title: Negotiate the whole package
docs.text: Component What to ask Base salary The main number; every future hike builds on it Joining / sign-on bonus Covers bonus or ESOPs you lose by leaving Variable / performance bonus Target %, how it's measured, how often it's paid out in practice ESOPs / RSUs Number, vesting schedule, cliff, current valuation Title / level Affects future pay and your next job Notice-period buyout If your current notice is long Remote / hybrid Days in office, home-office allowance Learning budget Certifications, conferences Review timeline Early review at 6 months Relocation Travel, temporary housing

docs.title: Phrases that help and phrases that hurt
docs.text: ❌ Avoid ✅ Use instead "I need more money because my rent went up." "Based on my impact and market data…" "Whatever you think is fair." "I'm looking for around ₹58 lakh." "I'll leave if I don't get it." (threat) "I want to grow here. What would make this possible?" "Sorry to ask, but…" "I'd like to discuss…" "Okay." (accepting immediately) "Thank you. Can I take a day to review the full package?" A single exact low number A researched range or a confident specific number

docs.title: Golden rules
docs.text:
Do

  • Be enthusiastic about the role and firm on the number in the same conversation.
  • Ask for time: "Can I get back to you by Thursday?" is normal.
  • Get everything in writing before you resign from your current job.
  • Negotiate once, well. Avoid going back again and again.

Don't

  • Lie about offers or current salary.
  • Negotiate over chat or messages for the main discussion; prefer a call.
  • Accept a counter-offer from your current employer purely for money. The reasons you wanted to leave usually remain.
  • Burn bridges if it doesn't work out: "Thank you for the offer. I'll have to decline this time, but I'd love to stay in touch."

docs.title: Practise with AI
docs.text:
Role-play a salary negotiation. You are an HR manager at a product company. Offer me ₹48 LPA for a
Senior Backend Engineer role (my target is ₹58 LPA, walk-away ₹50 LPA). Push back realistically:
"budget is fixed", "that's above our band", "we need an answer today". After I type DEBRIEF, score
my negotiation and rewrite my weakest reply.

See the Master Prompt for the full coaching setup.

docs.title: Everyday Life
docs.text:
Talking at the airport or on a train builds the same confidence you use at work. Each page lists the questions to ask, the questions you'll be asked, ready-made phrases, and what to do when things go wrong.

  • Airport

    Check-in, security, immigration, boarding, delays, lost bags.

    Open

  • Train

    Tickets, platforms, seats, ticket examiner, missed trains.

    Open

  • Hotel

    Check-in, room issues, requests, check-out.

    Open

  • Restaurant & Café

    Ordering, dietary needs, complaints, the bill.

    Open

  • Cab & Directions

    Booking, talking to drivers, asking strangers the way.

    Open

  • Doctor & Pharmacy

    Describing symptoms, asking about medicines.

    Open

  • Bank & Shopping

    Accounts, cards, returns, bargaining.

    Open

The universal formula for strangers

docs.title: At the Airport
docs.text: An airport is a series of short conversations with people who are busy. Have your documents ready, answer exactly what's asked, and don't be shy about asking for help.

docs.title: Your airport journey
docs.text: 1. Check-in & bag drop 2. Security screening 3. Immigration / passport control — international 4. Gate & boarding 5. On the plane 6. Arrival: immigration, baggage, customs

docs.title: 1. Check-in counter
docs.text:
What you'll be askedWhat you can ask They ask You answer "May I see your passport / ID and ticket, please?" "Sure, here you go." "Where are you flying to today?" "To Singapore, then connecting to Sydney." "How many bags are you checking in?" "Just one, and one cabin bag." "Did you pack your bags yourself?" "Yes, I did." "Are you carrying any batteries, power banks, or liquids in your checked bag?" "No, the power bank is in my cabin bag." "Window or aisle?" "Aisle, please." "Your bag is 3 kg over. There's an excess charge." "Could I move some items to my cabin bag instead?"
  • "Could I get an aisle / window seat, please?"
  • "Is it possible to sit together with my colleague?"
  • "Is my bag checked through to my final destination, or do I collect it in transit?"
  • "What time does boarding start, and which gate?"
  • "Is there any extra legroom / exit row seat available?"
  • "What's the baggage allowance on this ticket?"
  • "Can I add my frequent flyer number?"
  • "Is the flight on time?"

docs.title: 2. Security
docs.text:
You'll hear Meaning / what to do "Laptops and liquids out, please." Put laptop & liquids (≤100 ml, in a clear bag) in a separate tray "Anything in your pockets?" Wallet, phone, keys, coins go in the tray "Please remove your belt / shoes / jacket." Do it, place in tray "Step through, please. Arms up." Walk through the scanner / body scanner "Is this your bag? I need to check it." "Yes, sure, go ahead." Stay calm. Random checks are normal.

You can ask: "Do I need to take out my tablet / charger too?" · "Can I keep my shoes on?"

docs.title: 3. Immigration (international)
docs.text:
Golden rule

Answer only what's asked, honestly, briefly. Keep documents ready: passport, visa, return ticket, hotel booking, invitation letter.

Officer asks Good answer "What's the purpose of your visit?" "Business. I'm attending a tech conference." / "Tourism." "How long will you stay?" "Five days. I return on the 12th." "Where will you be staying?" "At the Marina Hotel, here's the booking." "Who is your employer / what do you do?" "I'm a senior software engineer at XYZ Technologies." "Have you been here before?" "Yes, once in 2024." / "No, first time." "Are you carrying more than [X] in cash?" "No." / "Yes, here's my declaration." "Do you have a return ticket?" "Yes, here it is."

If you don't understand: "Sorry, could you repeat that, please?" Don't guess.

docs.title: 4. At the gate & boarding
docs.text:
You can ask:

  • "Excuse me, is this the gate for the Mumbai flight?"
  • "Has boarding started for AI 302?"
  • "Is the flight delayed? Do you know the new time?"
  • "Which boarding group am I in?"
  • "Can I take this bag on board, or does it need to be gate-checked?"

Announcements decoded:

Announcement Meaning "Pre-boarding for families and passengers needing assistance" Not you yet (unless it applies) "Now boarding zones 1 and 2" Check your boarding pass zone/group "Final call for passenger…" Hurry! The gate is closing "Gate change" Check the screens, move to the new gate

docs.title: 5. On the plane
docs.text:
• "Excuse me, I think you're in my seat. I'm 14C." (show boarding pass, smile)
  • "Could you help me put my bag in the overhead bin?"
  • "Could I have a glass of water, please?"
  • "Is it possible to change seats? There's an empty one at the back."
  • "Excuse me, could I get past? Thank you."
  • "What time do we land (local time)?"

docs.title: 6. Arrival
docs.text:
BaggageLost / damaged bagCustoms
  • "Which belt is the bag from flight SQ 421 on?"
  • "Where is the baggage services / lost & found desk?"

"Hi, my bag didn't arrive on flight SQ 421 from Bangalore. Here's my baggage tag. It's a large black suitcase with a red ribbon. Could you file a report? When can I expect it, and can it be delivered to my hotel? Is there an allowance for essentials meanwhile?"

Always get a reference number (PIR) and a phone/email for follow-up.

Asked Answer "Anything to declare?" "No, nothing." / "Yes, I have [item]." "Are you carrying food items?" Be honest: "Yes, some packaged snacks."

docs.text:
Flight delayed / cancelledMissed connectionCan't find your gate / lost

"My flight to Delhi has been cancelled. What are my options? Can you rebook me on the next available flight? Will the airline provide a hotel / meal voucher? And can I get that in writing?"

"My first flight was delayed and I missed my connection to London. Here's my boarding pass. Can you put me on the next flight? Will my checked bag be transferred too?"

"Excuse me, I'm a bit lost. How do I get to the international transfers / Gate B12? Is it a long walk, or should I take the train?"

docs.text: Word Meaning Layover / Stopover A stop between flights (short / long) Transit / Transfer Changing planes Boarding pass The pass that lets you board Carry-on / Cabin bag Bag you take on the plane Checked baggage Bag that goes in the hold Excess baggage Weight over the allowance (fee) Departures / Arrivals Leaving / coming areas Duty-free Tax-free shops after security Jet lag Tiredness from time-zone change Red-eye Overnight flight

docs.title: Bank & Shopping
docs.text: When money is involved, be clear, confirm details, and get it in writing.

docs.title: At the bank
docs.text:
Need Say Open an account "I'd like to open a savings account. What documents do I need?" Card blocked "My card has been blocked after a failed transaction. Could you help me unblock it?" Wrong charge "There's a transaction I don't recognise: ₹4,500 on the 2nd. I'd like to raise a dispute." Transfer "I need to make an international transfer. What are the charges and exchange rate?" Loan "What's the interest rate for a home loan, and is it fixed or floating?" Fees "Are there any hidden charges or minimum balance requirements?"

Tip

Always ask: "Could I get a reference number for this request?" and "How long will it take?"

docs.title: Shopping
docs.text:
• "I'm just looking, thanks."
  • "Do you have this in a bigger / smaller size? In blue?"
  • "Can I try this on? Where's the fitting room?"
  • "Is there a discount on this?" / "Is this the final price?"
  • "What's the return / exchange policy?"
  • "Does it come with a warranty?"

docs.title: Returns & complaints
docs.text:
"Hi, I bought these headphones last week and the left side stopped working. Here's the receipt. I'd like a replacement or a refund, please."

If it's not resolved: "Could I speak to the manager, please?" Stay calm and polite, and repeat the facts.

docs.title: Bargaining (local markets)
docs.text:
1. "How much is this?"
  2. "Hmm, that's a bit much. Could you do ₹400?"
  3. "If I buy two, what's your best price?"
  4. Smile and walk away politely if it's too high: "Thanks, I'll think about it."

docs.title: Cab & Directions
docs.text: Confirm, clarify, stay safe. Short, clear phrases work best with drivers and strangers.

docs.title: Booking / starting a ride
docs.text:
• "Hi, are you here for Ashish? Going to Terminal 2?" (confirm the driver before you get in)
  • "Can you follow the map, please?"
  • "How long will it take with this traffic?"
  • "Could you turn the AC up / down, please?"
  • "Could you stop here, please? Just after the signal."
  • "Could you wait 5 minutes? I need to pick up a bag."

docs.title: Taxi without an app (fixed fare)
docs.text:
• "How much to the railway station?"
  • "Do you use the meter?"
  • "That seems high. Could you do ₹300?"

docs.title: Asking for directions
docs.text:
"Excuse me, sorry to bother you. How do I get to the Central Library? Is it walking distance?"

Ask Useful when "Is it far from here?" Deciding walk vs cab "Which way is the metro station?" Need a direction "Is there a bus that goes there?" Public transport "Can you show me on the map?" Directions are complicated "So, straight, then left at the bank. Right?" Confirming (repeat back!)

Direction vocabulary: go straight · turn left/right · take the second left · at the signal/roundabout · opposite · next to · around the corner · cross the road.

docs.title: Safety phrases
docs.text:
• "Please don't take a different route without asking me."
  • "I'm sharing my live location with my family."
  • "Please stop the car. I'd like to get out here."

docs.title: Doctor & Pharmacy
docs.text: Being precise with a doctor is like writing a good bug report: symptoms, when it started, how bad it is, and what makes it better or worse.

docs.title: The "health bug report"
docs.text:
What:      sore throat and fever (101°F)
Since:     2 days, started Tuesday night
Severity:  pain 6/10 when swallowing
Pattern:   worse at night
Tried:     paracetamol — helps for ~4 hours
Other:     no allergies; I take blood-pressure medicine (amlodipine)

docs.title: At the doctor's
docs.text:
Describing symptoms:

  • "I've had a headache for three days."
  • "It's a sharp / dull / throbbing / burning pain."
  • "It hurts when I bend down / swallow / breathe deeply."
  • "I feel dizzy / nauseous / tired all the time."
  • "I'm allergic to penicillin."

Questions to ask the doctor:

  • "What do you think is causing this?"
  • "Is it serious? Is it contagious?"
  • "How often should I take this medicine, and for how long?"
  • "Are there any side effects I should watch for?"
  • "Can I work / travel / exercise?"
  • "When should I come back if it doesn't get better?"
  • "Do I need any tests?"

docs.title: At the pharmacy
docs.text:
• "I have a prescription for this."
  • "Do you have something for a cough / cold / acidity?"
  • "Is this safe to take with my blood-pressure medicine?"
  • "Should I take it before or after food?"
  • "Is there a generic / cheaper version?"

docs.title: Emergencies
docs.text:
Emergency phrases

"I need an ambulance. Someone has collapsed at [exact address / landmark]." "Please call a doctor, it's urgent." "Where is the nearest hospital / emergency room?"

India: 112 (all emergencies) · 108 (ambulance in many states). Abroad: learn the local emergency number before you travel (e.g. 911 US, 112 EU, 999 UK).

docs.title: At the Hotel
docs.text: Polite + specific = fast service. Front-desk staff solve problems all day. Make yours easy to solve.

docs.title: Check-in
docs.text:
They ask You say "Do you have a reservation?" "Yes, under the name Ashish Gupta, for 3 nights." "May I see your ID and a card for incidentals?" "Sure. Is the deposit refundable at check-out?" "Would you like breakfast included?" "How much extra is it per day?"

You can ask:

  • "Is early check-in possible? My flight landed early."
  • "What time is check-out? Is late check-out available?"
  • "What's the Wi-Fi password?"
  • "What time is breakfast, and where?"
  • "Could I have a quiet room / high floor / away from the lift?"
  • "Is there an airport shuttle? What time does it leave?"
  • "Do you have a gym / laundry service / business centre?"
  • "Can I leave my luggage here after check-out?"

docs.title: Problems with the room
docs.text:
"Hi, this is room 512. The AC isn't cooling, and the room is quite warm. Could you send someone to check it, or move me to another room? Thank you."

Other requests:

  • "Could I get extra towels / pillows, please?"
  • "The hot water isn't working."
  • "There's a lot of noise from the next room. Could you help?"
  • "I booked a non-smoking room, but this one smells of smoke."

docs.title: Check-out
docs.text:
• "I'd like to check out. Room 512."
  • "Could I see an itemised bill? I don't think I used the minibar."
  • "Could you send the invoice to my email with my company's name and GST number?"
  • "Could you call a cab to the airport, please?"

docs.title: Phone Calls
docs.text: Phone calls are harder than face-to-face talk because you can't see the other person. Prepare 3 bullet points, speak slowly, and confirm everything at the end.

docs.title: Before you call
docs.text:
• Write your goal: "Reschedule appointment to Friday."
  • Have details ready: booking ID, account number, dates
  • Have pen & paper for reference numbers
  • Find a quiet place

docs.title: Opening the call
docs.text: "Hi, this is Ashish Gupta. I'm calling about my booking, reference 4X7Q2. I'd like to change the date to Friday the 14th."

docs.title: Useful phrases
docs.text: Situation Say Didn't hear "Sorry, the line's not clear. Could you repeat that?" Spelling "Could you spell that for me?" / "That's G for Goa, U for Umbrella…" Numbers "Let me read that back: 9-8-4-5…" Put on hold "Sure, I'll hold." Wrong department "Could you transfer me to the billing team, please?" Getting nowhere "I understand. Could I speak to a supervisor, please?" Ending "Just to confirm: the appointment is Friday at 3 pm, ref 4X7Q2. Thank you!"

docs.title: Work calls
docs.text:
• Start: "Hi Rahul, is now a good time? It'll take 5 minutes."
  • Unexpected call: "Can I call you back in 10 minutes? I'm just finishing something."
  • End: "Great, I'll send a quick email summarising what we agreed."

docs.title: Leaving a voicemail
docs.text:
"Hi, this is Ashish Gupta from XYZ Technologies. I'm calling about the invoice for October.
Please call me back on 98450-12345. Again, that's 98450-12345. Thanks!"

Name → reason → number (said twice, slowly) → thanks.

docs.title: Restaurant & Café
docs.text: Ordering food is a good confidence workout: short, friendly and low-risk. Team dinners and client lunches use the same phrases.

docs.title: Arriving
docs.text:
• "A table for two, please."
  • "We have a reservation under Gupta, 8 pm."
  • "Could we sit by the window / outside / somewhere quieter?"
  • "How long is the wait?"

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: Situation Say Need time "Could we have a few more minutes, please?" Ask for a recommendation "What do you recommend? What's popular here?" Dietary needs "I'm vegetarian / vegan / allergic to peanuts. Does this dish contain any?" Customise "Could I have this less spicy / without onions / sauce on the side?" Ordering "I'll have the paneer tikka, and could I get a lime soda?" Portion "Is this enough for two, or should we order more?" Coffee "A medium cappuccino with oat milk, please. For here / to go."

docs.title: During the meal
docs.text:
• "Excuse me, could we get some more water, please?"
  • "Sorry, this isn't what I ordered. I asked for the grilled fish."
  • "The food is a bit cold. Could you warm it up, please?"
  • "Everything was delicious, thank you!"

docs.title: The bill
docs.text:
• "Could we have the bill / the check, please?"
  • "Can we split the bill?" / "I'll get this one."
  • "Do you accept cards / UPI?"
  • "Is service charge included?"

Hosting a client / team dinner

Let guests order first. Suggest 2–3 dishes if they're unsure. Avoid heavy work talk until the food arrives. Settle the bill quietly (tell the waiter in advance, or step away to pay).

docs.title: Small Talk & Networking
docs.text: Small talk is how people start to trust each other. Most opportunities (jobs, partnerships, mentors) start with a 3-minute chat. Ask, listen, follow up.

docs.title: The 4-step conversation
docs.text: 1. Open — comment on the shared situation 2. Ask — open questions about them 3. Connect — find something in common, share a little 4. Exit — gracefully, with a next step

docs.title: Openers
docs.text:
Conference / meetupOffice / new teamTravel (airport, train, flight)Waiting / lift / café
  • "Hi, I'm Ashish. What did you think of that talk?"
  • "What brings you here today?"
  • "Is this your first time at this conference?"
  • "Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm Ashish, I work on the checkout team."
  • "How was your weekend?"
  • "Are you working on anything exciting this quarter?"
  • "Are you travelling for work or holiday?"
  • "Have you been to Singapore before? Any tips?"
  • "This delay is long, isn't it? Where are you heading?"
  • "Busy day today, isn't it?"
  • "That smells great. What did you order?"

docs.title: Keep it going: the FORD topics
docs.text:
Topic Question Family / home "Are you from Bangalore originally?" Occupation "What kind of work do you do?" → "What do you enjoy most about it?" Recreation "What do you do when you're not working?" Dreams "What are you excited about this year?"

Follow-up magic phrases: "Oh, how did you get into that?" · "That's interesting, tell me more." · "What was that like?"

docs.title: Introduce yourself (networking pitch)
docs.text:
"I'm Ashish. I'm a backend engineer working on a grocery marketplace. Lots of Kafka and microservices. Lately I've been figuring out how to make checkout reliable during flash sales. What about you?"

Keep it short and interesting, and end with a question back to them.

docs.title: Exiting politely
docs.text:
• "It was great talking to you. I'm going to grab a coffee before the next session."
  • "I don't want to keep you. Can we connect on LinkedIn?"
  • "Let me introduce you to Priya. She's working on exactly that."

docs.title: Follow up within 24 hours
docs.text:
Hi Neha, great meeting you at the Kafka Summit yesterday! I really enjoyed our chat about
consumer lag. Here's the blog post I mentioned: [link]. Would love to stay in touch.
— Ashish

docs.title: Topics to avoid with strangers / at work
docs.text: Politics · religion · salary · weight/appearance · gossip about colleagues.

docs.title: On the Train
docs.text: Railway stations are busy, loud and quick. Ask early, confirm twice, and keep your ticket and ID ready. These phrases work in India and abroad.

docs.title: At the ticket counter / enquiry
docs.text:
You can ask:

  • "One ticket to Pune, please. Second AC / sleeper / general?" (India)
  • "A return ticket to Manchester, please. Off-peak if possible." (UK)
  • "What time is the next train to Chennai?"
  • "Is it a direct train, or do I need to change?"
  • "Which platform does it leave from?"
  • "How long does the journey take?"
  • "Is there a cheaper option / railcard / senior discount?"
  • "Can I cancel or change this ticket later? Is there a fee?"

docs.title: At the station
docs.text: Ask When "Excuse me, is this the right platform for the Shatabdi to Mysore?" Before boarding "Has the platform changed?" When boards/announcements are confusing "Is the train running late?" Check delays "Where does coach B3 stop on the platform?" Long trains (India) "Where's the waiting room / cloakroom / lift?" Facilities "Does this train stop at Kalyan?" Confirm stops

Your seatCo-passengersTicket examiner (TTE / conductor)
  • "Excuse me, I think this is my seat: 32, coach S4." (show ticket politely)
  • "Would you mind swapping seats? I'd like to sit with my family."
  • "Is this seat taken?" (unreserved trains)
  • "Could you help me lift my bag onto the rack?"
  • "Do you mind if I open / close the window?"

  • "Could you keep an eye on my bag for two minutes?"

They ask / say You say "Ticket, please." "Here you go." (ticket + ID) "Your ticket is waitlisted / RAC." "Is there any berth available now? Could you allot one, please?" "You're in the wrong coach." "Sorry, which coach should I go to?" "This ticket isn't valid on this train." "I'm sorry, I didn't realise. What are my options? Can I pay the difference?"

Missed the trainTrain cancelled / very lateLost item

"Hi, I just missed the 6:15 train to Bangalore. Can I use this ticket on the next one, or do I need a new ticket? Can I get a partial refund?"

"The 9 am train is cancelled. Is there an alternative train or bus? How do I claim a refund?"

"I left my laptop bag on the train that arrived at platform 4 at 10:30, coach A1, seat 22. It's a black backpack. Where is the lost-property office, or who can I report it to?"

docs.title: Foundations
docs.text:
Every script in this playbook rests on these pages. Beginners: read them in order. Experienced folks: skim them, then do the self-assessment in the 90-day plan.

  • Communication Principles

    Clarity, structure, tone, and adapting to your audience. The 7 rules behind every good conversation.

    Read
